summary: Describes where RDMAP and DDP apply. It compares transport options for DDP, advises upper layer developers on choosing among them, and compares DDP with direct use of the transports and with non-IP RDMA. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5045 explains when Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) and Direct Data Placement (DDP) can help applications. It compares transport choices and describes limits that application designers must consider.

questions: what are tagged and untagged messages in ddp
subtitle: When direct data placement helps and how SCTP and TCP differ beneath it.

tldr.problem: Application designers need to know when RDMAP and DDP help more than using TCP or SCTP directly, and which transport best fits their needs.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains tagged and untagged messages, RDMA Reads, flow-control assumptions and trade-offs between SCTP, MPA/TCP and non-IP transports.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5045 is Informational guidance rather than a protocol definition; the supplied metadata says RFC 7146 updates it.

today: RFC 5045 is an Informational RFC published in October 2007 and has been updated by RFC 7146. It provides applicability guidance rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: What RDMAP and DDP Provide
sections.content:
DDP places received application data directly into buffers selected by an upper-layer protocol (ULP). RDMAP provides completion notifications and RDMA Reads, which let a data sink fetch from an advertised buffer.

DDP can run over IP transports including SCTP and TCP. The RFC is guidance about when these services are useful compared with direct use of an underlying transport; it notes that applications must be designed to use the capabilities.
sections.plainLanguage: One protocol places incoming data in a buffer chosen by the application. Its companion reports completion and lets the receiver fetch data from an advertised buffer.

sections.title: Tagged and Untagged Messages
sections.content:
A Tagged Message carries addressing information that identifies a buffer chosen by the sender; the receiver gets no separate notification for each tagged message. An Untagged Message is matched to a buffer the receiver supplied in advance, and the receiver is notified when it arrives.

The ULP controls how peers advertise buffers. The memo says tagged messages can carry data while untagged messages can carry control, but a ULP cannot rely entirely on tagged messages because it needs a way to confirm delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: In a tagged message, the sender identifies the destination buffer. In an untagged message, the receiver chooses the buffer and receives a notification.

sections.title: Data Placement and RDMA Reads
sections.content:
Tagged messages let a sender choose the order and packetization of data placed in advertised buffers. RDMAP can combine completion notifications for tagged messages with a following untagged message, reducing ULP interactions; this can delay processing until the full exchange is placed.

RDMA Reads let a receiver fetch the portion of an advertised buffer it needs. The memo says this can suit storage systems that limit write buffers, but it is less suitable when the ULP needs atomic consistency across multiple updates.
sections.plainLanguage: Tagged data can arrive in an order chosen by the sender, and a later notification can confirm completion of the exchange. An RDMA Read lets the receiver request only the part of a buffer it needs.

sections.title: Choosing SCTP or MPA/TCP
sections.content:
SCTP preserves message boundaries and can carry multiple DDP streams in one association. With TCP, the MPA adaptation layer provides DDP framing; to network middleboxes, MPA/TCP traffic appears as a normal TCP connection.

Both adaptations provide end-to-end CRC32c protection against accidental corruption. SCTP always provides this protection; MPA/TCP must implement it but can disable it administratively only when equivalent or better end-to-end protection exists. The ULP chooses the transport.
sections.plainLanguage: One transport preserves message boundaries; the other needs an adaptation layer to frame messages. Both provide an end-to-end error check, which can be disabled only when equivalent protection exists.

sections.title: Flow Control and Buffer Exposure
sections.content:
DDP defines no standard flow control. It relies on the ULP to manage untagged-message credits and on the lower-layer transport for reliable delivery and congestion control; without transport flow control, the RFC warns of severe congestion.

Only ULP actions expose memory, but DDP and RDMAP do not report whether a peer writes to the wrong advertised buffer. The memo suggests using distinct steering tags and invalidating them after use when peers do not have an adequate basis for mutual trust.
sections.plainLanguage: The ULP must control how many untagged messages a peer may send, and the transport must provide reliable service and congestion control. Applications must also manage which buffers a peer can access.
